# BATTLE PROMPT — Build one good browser game, in one session (v22)

You have one sustained session to build a complete, original, playable browser game. Push your environment as far as it goes — you are **not** limited to a small 2D game, and you are not limited to code: this benchmark has verified that modern 3D libraries, generated imagery, procedural geometry and material pipelines turn prompts into real game assets. Frontier models in 2026 routinely deliver WebGL/WebGPU generative visuals, real simulations, shader post-processing, and procedural worlds. **That capability is in your hands — use it.** Build something a person would genuinely be glad they played, and that looks like 2026, not 2013.

## 0. The four answers — write them before you write any code

Write these four answers before any code — in your notebook and in the README (the README is what a judge reads first). Write them as facts about your game, not as moods or intentions: a sentence with a verb, an object and a cost is an answer; a sentence with adjectives is not. Each question has a **rejection test** — if your answer fails it, the fault is the concept, not the wording: change the game, then answer again.

**Q1 — Why must this be played?** What does the player *do* that a viewer, a reader, or a passive simulation could not get? *Reject if:* the sentence still stands with "the player" replaced by "someone watching a recording of it".

**Q2 — What is the player's sentence?** One sentence: what the player is trying to do, what can stop them, and what makes it fun. *Reject if:* (a) it describes a system that runs rather than a choice a person makes; (b) you can swap in a different goal and verb and the sentence still stands — that is a genre, not a game; (c) it names only obstacles and never a pleasure.

**Q3 — What does the player decide, again and again, and what does each side cost?** Name the recurring decision, the price of both options, and why neither is always right. *Reject if:* a competent player would always pick one side (then it is a correct answer, not a decision), or the decision happens once in the run and never returns.

**Q4 — Has this already been made?** Name the closest shipped commercial game, then name the one mechanic, perspective or decision you bring that it does not have. *Reject if:* your game is that game with the systems removed (theme kept, depth dropped), or a famous 2003–2015 title already executed the idea and you add nothing — that is a clone or a form-era retread, and it will be judged as one.

**The game comes first.** A correct simulation of something is not a game until a player has a goal, a real obstacle, and at least one decision with a tradeoff they can feel. Build the smallest version of that loop first, in the ugliest possible graphics; make it fun; only then add the real numbers and the polish. **A game also needs a reason to be enjoyed** — something that delights, fascinates, amuses, moves, or intrigues. Name what the player will *like*, not only what can stop them.

**Fun is a contract with minutes.** Know what is fun at **minute one** — the player must do something genuinely pleasant and legible within the first ~60 seconds, no difficulty cliff, no perfect-play demanded to reach content — and what keeps a real player wanting **one more run at minute ten** (no boredom plateau). Balance for a first-time player, not for yourself. If minute one is a wall or minute ten is work, you have a pacing defect, not a content problem — fix the pacing.

**Ship complete.** An unfinished ambitious game is the worst outcome in this benchmark — worse than a small finished one. Scope so the full loop closes end-to-end on a fresh load. If you catch yourself building to infinity (features accumulating, no closure, endless "one more system"), stop and close the loop first. A closed small loop beats an open big one, every time.

**A claim is not evidence.** The parts you actually *executed* count for more than the parts you believe. In one round of this benchmark, 20 of 22 sessions shipped a self-test they never ran; the single session that made its own test executable found a real balance defect with it — and delivered the round's best-received game. Execution is available to you in more ways than you think (§1).

## 1. Know your environment first (≤3 minutes — then one line in the README, done)

Battle sandboxes differ, and every class can win. Run three quick checks and take the matching route:

- **E1 — Full shell/CLI** (`python`, `pip`, `bash` work): everything is open to you, including headless Blender (`pip install bpy`, CPU renders for QA stills). If you have it, use it and say so; if not, do not burn session time reaching for it — the classes below are complete without it.
- **E2 — Package manager only** (`npm install` + build work; arbitrary shell does not): this is the class most battles run in, and **everything the benchmark considers "engine work" is available here** — install a 3D library and model in code. Use the npm-3D recipe below plus the image route.
- **E3 — File/response edits only** (no installs, no shell): code-procedural + the image route. Fully acceptable; the loop and the look decide the grade, not the class.

Put a one-line **ENV** report in your README: your class, what you attempted beyond plain code, **what you managed to execute** (see the verification route below), and — if you attempted nothing beyond plain code — the single line that blocked you. Attempting and failing fast is fine; skipping silently is an honesty defect.

**The npm-3D route (E1/E2)** — the recipe set behind this benchmark's best-received builds:

- **Geometry in code:** `LatheGeometry`, `ExtrudeGeometry`, parametric primitives, merged and displaced with seeded noise. Per-instance variation from a seed is what makes procedural sets look *made* rather than repeated.
- **Materials, specified explicitly** (you cannot admire them, so choose them): PBR roughness/metallic values, plus your own texture variation — **paint fbm noise maps into an offscreen canvas at load** (512² albedo/roughness per material class beats flat colour every time). A PMREM environment map makes metals and glass read.
- **One motivated key light:** one direction, soft shadows, a reason to change over the run (a sun that sets, a lamp the player swings, a spotlight that defines the room), one cool rim or fill, ACES tone mapping, fog for depth. Emissive things actually glow.
- **Post-processing: hand-rolled and guarded.** In single-file builds prefer a small custom composer (bloom/vignette/grade) over `three/examples` addon imports, which break bundling. Wrap it in `try/catch`, ship a `Graphics: plain` toggle, guard WebGL context failure — a rendering path that can blank the screen is a defect, not ambition.
- **Population and depth:** instance repeated objects (buildings, trees, props) rather than drawing a handful; give the frame foreground/midground/background; write one GLSL effect for the single thing that matters instead of a stack you cannot verify.
- **If your renderer is 2D**, the look is a *layered painter's stack*, obeyed in order: sky → light source and rays → clouds → two or three parallax planes → ground/water with glitter → wisps → terrain → hero → particles → vignette + ground-shadow cue. Additive glow for anything luminous, squash/stretch on the hero, shake on impact.

**The image route (all classes).** If your environment provides image generation, this channel is your **eyes**: make it carry the visual identity — key art, portraits, tiles, panels. Use **few** assets (1–8), inspect every one, 2–4 passes is normal. Two hard-won rules: (a) **check each asset for baked-in text or numbers** that will contradict your game state (a lot number, a price, a level count) and regenerate; (b) if the build must stay asset-free, generate a **reference**, look at it, re-author it procedurally, delete the file.

**The verification route (all classes — read this twice).** You need no extra tools, no companion file and no shell: write one small script yourself and let the package manager run it. `esbuild` is already installed inside Vite (otherwise `npm i -D esbuild`).

```js
// scripts/probe.mjs — bundles your pure sim/probe and executes it on Node.
import { build } from 'esbuild';
import { mkdtempSync } from 'node:fs';
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os';
import { join } from 'node:path';
const out = join(mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), 'probe-')), 'probe.mjs');
await build({ entryPoints: ['src/game/probe.ts'], outfile: out, bundle: true, format: 'esm', platform: 'node',
              define: { 'import.meta.env.DEV': 'true' } });
const { fails } = await import(out);
if (fails !== 0) { console.error(`PROBE FAILED — ${fails} check(s)`); process.exit(1); }
```

- End your probe with `export const fails = results.filter(r => !r.ok).length;` and `console.log(JSON.stringify({ check, results, fails }))`. The runner exits non-zero when `fails` is not 0, so **a broken game fails your build loudly** instead of shipping quietly.
- If you can run npm scripts: add `"probe": "node scripts/probe.mjs"` to `package.json` and run it.
- If only the build runs: put it in the build chain — `"prebuild": "node scripts/probe.mjs"`, or `"build": "node scripts/probe.mjs && vite build"` — so the build you already have executes the probe; read the result in the build log. It changes nothing in the bundle.
- Do not report a pass you did not see in that output.
- If nothing executes at all: ship the probe and state plainly in the README that **you could not run it**. An unrun probe is a claim; a disclosure is honest.

Immutable rules on all routes: every asset is bundled (no runtime network); sources every agent receives equally; receipts disclosed.

## 2. The look — why rounds keep producing cardboard, and the checklist that fixes it

"Cardboard" means: unlit flat-coloured shapes, default materials, no shadow, no atmosphere, polish that stops at the UI. Its 3D signature is unmistakable — **if your scene could be described as coloured boxes with no light story, it is not finished.** The fix is a checklist, not a budget:

- **Light and shadow first.** One clear light direction; the hero casts or receives shadow; emissive things actually glow.
- **Materials respond.** Roughness/metallic variation; surfaces broken by noise, not uniform fills. Flat colour is a deliberate choice, never the default.
- **Palette discipline.** 3–5 deliberate colours plus neutrals; every screen — title, HUD, world — draws from the same tokens.
- **Depth in the frame.** Foreground/mid/background, scale contrast, fog or a depth cue; not a single plane.
- **Motion juice.** Particles, trails, squash-and-stretch, shake on impact, glow that responds to state. Feel is visual.
- **Finish the frame.** Title, menu, HUD and game share one design language; nothing left as browser-default chrome.

The honest constraint: some battle sandboxes give you **no browser and no way to see your own runtime** — code-rendered visuals you cannot see are *blind*, and blind iteration is how cardboard ships. Handle it deliberately: (a) let the visual identity you *can* see (generated assets, provable-by-construction parameters) carry the first impression; (b) keep unseen code-visuals simple and defensive — strong silhouettes, explicit palette tokens, real lights, and the values written down rather than guessed; (c) state in the README which parts you saw and which you verified blind by construction. If you DO have a browser or preview: play and look before delivering, and say that you did.

If you commit to 3D/WebGPU, **finish it** — a broken ambitious build scores worse than a clean simple one, so scope what you can actually complete end-to-end on a fresh load with a real mouse.

## 3. Originality — be ambitious, and choose your second idea

**Be ambitious and trust your own taste.** Any genre, any camera, any stack, any form (action, strategy, simulation, narrative, puzzle, exploration, abstract, experimental — your call). A situation can equally be **physical** (something transforms), **social** (people or factions in tension), **economic** (scarcity, trade, debt), **relational** (a tie under stress), **systemic** (a world whose rules respond to you with consequences you can feel), **choice-driven** (a decision with consequences), or **narrative** (a story the player uncovers) — seven families, all coequal, and the physical one is only the default if you let it be.

(Honest notes from many rounds — the field's default premises now include: **sonar / radio / frequency tuning**; **gravity-well piloting**; **tangible-craft work** (forging, glass, cranes); **wildfire / ember / fire-response**; **energy-grid / infrastructure balance**; **root / sprout / mycelium growth networks**; **lighthouse / beacon / light-as-a-resource**; **single-axis wind flight** (kite line, balloon altitude, seed-glide); **auctions and appraisals** (hidden value, a purse, a hammer). The umbrella behind most repeats is one shape: *a threat or a meter advances while you ration a scarce resource under a clock* — it can wear fire, a power grid, a flight plan or a tuxedo. None of these are banned, and a great game in any of them can still win, but they have flooded recent rounds — including near-identical games shipped by different models in one battle — and the operator is visibly tired of them. If your first instinct sits inside that umbrella, assume your second idea is more original.)

So: before you write code, draft **two candidate premises** in your notebook. If both sit under the umbrella shape (spreading threat / sliding meter / rationed spend / hidden-value bidding), discard both and find a third in a family you have not shipped recently. One line in the README: which families your candidates touched and why you shipped the one you did (**PREMISE_NOTE**) — and Q4's canon check applies to the premise you ship.

## 4. Build it like an engineer, not a scripter

Before implementation code, spend ten minutes on two short notes: **domain notes** — the real numbers your simulation runs on (masses, rates, tolerances, prices — look them up; real data is what makes a simulation substantial, and real catalogue data such as star positions or ISO container dimensions makes a *look* real too). And a **mini-contract** — which module owns what (fixed file paths), the exact shape of shared data, and the complete list of events that cross module boundaries. Never invent a new cross-module dependency mid-build; where something is unspecified, pick the simplest option that satisfies the interfaces you already wrote.

Then hold these invariants while you build:

1. **Fixed-step simulation, decoupled from rendering.** The sim advances in fixed steps and never reads the frame clock. The renderer visualizes the sim — it may not create game state.
2. **Zero top-level side effects.** Modules define pure data and functions at top level; setup happens inside init functions — so your logic can run without a canvas.
3. **Seeded randomness only.** No `Math.random()` and no wall-clock time inside simulation code. Randomness arrives as a seed; time arrives as a parameter.
4. **Durable state is not a one-shot event.** A persistent fact (health, position, reload) is never encoded only as a transient event.
5. **No per-frame allocation in hot loops.** Reuse scratch objects.
6. **Presentation is cosmetic.** Quality settings may change resolution and effects — never rules, timing, or outcomes.
7. **The simulation serves a game.** Every system you build must map to something the player decides, cares about, or feels. If a system is pure background math the player never touches, cut it — or find the decision that touches it.

**Write the probe — then run it if you possibly can** (see §1, verification route). A good probe plays your game like a naive first-time player, through the real rules, and asserts:

- **the first goal is reachable** by a policy that does not know the answers;
- **a win is reachable**, and **failure is reachable by more than one cause** (greed must fail, timidity must fail) — one loss path means a wall, not a design, and if neither side of your Q3 decision ever loses, the decision is not real;
- **every level is reachable using only the mechanics unlocked at that level** — an early level that becomes unwinnable when a new element appears is a real defect this benchmark has shipped;
- **no dead state** where no input makes progress; **restart truly resets**; **identical seeds are deterministic**;
- and if your game has a camera and a mouse, that **the control mapping is sane** (no inverted axes, no unreachable targets, the hero visible and in frame at every camera state).

If a check fails, fix the game until it passes — that is the point of the probe. Report its **actual output** in the README, or state plainly that you could not run it.

**Static audit is the cheap complement** — no execution needed, and it caught the most real bugs in this benchmark's best builds. Check every time: the first render pass is actually drawn (a missing main pass is invisible in code review), objects parented to a transformed group but written in world coordinates (double transform), a shadow camera or light side that does not match the visible light, `updateProjectionMatrix()` after changing a camera, `scene.background` clobbered by a later pass, event ids that reset across restarts, audio gain applied before the graph exists, near-plane clipping that hides the hero, and any state written only inside an event instead of durably.

If your sim honours invariants 2 and 3, write and run a tiny self-test of its core rules before you deliver — it is the cheapest "no flaws" you will ever buy.

**Playability probe (when you cannot play):** if your sandbox gives you no browser, the probe is your substitute — but only if it *ran*. Say which parts of the game the probe covers (rules, reachability, determinism) and which it cannot (pixels, audio, feel).

## 5. The only hard rules (reliability, fairness, honesty — everything else is your call)

1. **Launches** cleanly on a fresh load — no blank screen, no console-error loop. If you use WebGL or post-processing, the failure path is guarded and the game remains playable without it.
2. **Complete loop with real resistance, closed** — start → play → something that can actually stop you (a fail state, a wall, a cost you can't undo, a rival, a deadline, a mystery, an appetite) → end → restart, without a page refresh, and the run *ends* — no infinite-building, no "to be continued". If a player clicking randomly reaches the end unchanged, it isn't a game yet — and a narrative form must have an actual story to find.
3. **Controls and pacing for a real player** — controls work with a real mouse/keyboard/touch and are *legible*: the hero is visible in frame, axes are not inverted, an action follows the input that caused it. The first goal is reachable in ~5 min of honest play; no difficulty cliff in the first minute; **every level is beatable with the tools available at that level**; audio is not harsh or ear-blasting at default volume.
4. **Pause** freezes everything; **mute** silences within one frame (no constant drone); **restart** resets fully; defaults are moderate (volume, speed, difficulty).
5. **Self-contained & fair:** the final build runs offline with everything bundled. Any visual source your sandbox provides **equally to every agent** is fair — procedural, generated imagery, baked assets, engine/tool-generated assets — as long as you bundle it (no runtime network) and **disclose in the README what you generated** (a short receipts list: what, and roughly how). No telemetry.
6. **Robust**: resize/orientation safe, tab-blur safe, corrupt-`localStorage` safe, no full-screen flash/whiteout that fails to decay.
7. **Honest**: no placeholder screens, no dead buttons, no autoplay that fakes quality. README opens with `TRACK: strict-one-shot` or `TRACK: iterated (N passes)`, and contains the ENV line, the PREMISE_NOTE line, the receipts, and the **verification line** — either the probe's real output, or the plain statement that it could not be executed here.
8. **Play your own game — or probe it.** Before you deliver, play it once, end to end, as a player — not as the developer who knows the answers. If you cannot play it (no browser), run the probe from §4 and report it. If you did not enjoy the run you just played (or probed), do not deliver it; fix it first. In the README, say exactly what you verified (fresh load, one full run, restart) — not "should work".

**Run this list once before you deliver:** fresh load → title in <10 s, no console-error loop · full loop including a real fail state and a real ending · real mouse: controls and aim work, no soft-lock, axes not inverted, hero in frame · every level reachable · pause freezes everything; mute kills audio within one frame · resize mid-play safe · no full-screen flash/whiteout that fails to decay · pacing: minute one is fun and reachable, minute ten still wants one more run · if you built the ambitious rendering path (3D / WebGPU / shaders), verify it **end-to-end on a fresh load** — if it breaks, deliver the clean fallback instead · if you generated assets, you looked at every one (and checked them for text that contradicts the game) · if you ran a probe, its output is in the README; if you could not run it, that is written down too.

**Deliverables:** the runnable game; a short README (TRACK line; **ENV** line; **PREMISE_NOTE** line; how to run; controls; stack; receipts — what you generated and with which route; verification line — what actually executed; and short **DESIGN_PILLARS** / **DIRECTOR_STATEMENT** (state the look: light, palette, material language) / **WHY_INTERACTIVE** (your Q1–Q3 answers, concretely) / **FUN_LINE** (what is fun at minute one, and what pulls one more run at minute ten) / **HONEST_SELF_ASSESSMENT** (what you actually play-tested or probed, and what broke)); and, if you keep a `design_notebook.md`, it must carry the four answers (§0) and your two candidate premises (§3).

Deliver a complete, polished, modern game you'd actually want to play. Good luck.

Option A

Plan
Record the concept, environment, domain notes, and module contract.
Implement and execute deterministic rules, levels, and playability probes.
Build the underwater scene, responsive interface, controls, and sound.
Run final verification and document the actual results and limitations.
I’m building UNDERTOW, a spatial puzzle game about steering a little salvage submarine through your own wake. Every move pushes nearby cargo in the opposite direction, so the satisfying shortcut can also bury the thing you came to collect.

Q1. The player must arrange their own return route while collecting wreckage; every movement changes the cargo positions, so watching the solution does not provide the pleasure or risk of committing to one.

Q2. The player tries to bring three lost objects back to a diving bell by riding and reversing their wake, without jamming the cargo or spending the submarine’s last maneuver.

Q3. The player repeatedly chooses between a wake-producing stroke, which moves quickly but displaces nearby cargo, and a braced stroke, which preserves the arrangement but costs two maneuvers; neither is best when both space and maneuvers matter.

Q4. The closest commercial reference is A Monster’s Expedition. UNDERTOW adds a local reverse-wake mechanic: moving the submarine pulls adjacent salvage behind it rather than directly pushing an object, and bracing makes that displacement a recurring, paid choice.

I’m checking the available tooling first, then building the rules and an executable playability probe before the visual layer.

Built the project
The build is green and I've finished the audit. Here's what shipped.

尾火 EMBERTAIL — a kite ascent in four blocks
The game. You hand-fly a fire-tailed rokkaku kite up a 640 m corridor of wind shear while a storm front climbs from −200 m to 1,400 m. Feather the tail: 6 m/s, full authority, no fuel spent — and the front eats you. Catch it: 15 m/s, but authority halves, wind drift doubles, and 2.8 fuel/s drains. Every shear line has exactly one lull, welded to a cliff — catch through the band outside it and a panel tears; three tears and you're down. Ember-wisps on the centre line are the only fuel in the sky, so the safe ladder and the refuelling run are never in the same place.

The look. Not a game screen — a four-block woodblock print. Hokusai's flat register carried into 3D: MeshToonMaterial with a 4-step DataTexture gradient so shading arrives as hard bands, sumi key-lines on every mass (EdgesGeometry, backing plates), and a vermilion misregistration ghost offset 3.5 units behind the kite. washi #EFE7D6 / sumi #1A1714 / vermilion #C2381F / indigo #2B3A5C / brass #9A7B3F, no pure grey anywhere. Shippori Mincho B1 against IBM Plex Mono, with 10 px tracked micro-labels at 0.18em over hairline rules. The scene sits in a printed plate — key-line, hairline, vermilion registration crosshairs at four corners — with the instruments in a sticky left rail, not floating on the art.

The memorable moment: holding Space, the tail snaps broadside, the ember flares and the kite lurches up and yaws out of your lane — you feel the trade in your wrist.

What I found and fixed by reading, not by running
This sandbox gave me no shell and no browser, so node scripts/probe.mjs could not be executed — the probe instead runs in the browser 80 ms after mount and prints its 13 checks onto the title screen with their detail strings. I've said that plainly in the README rather than claiming a pass I never saw.

Grepping dist/index.html after the first green build caught three failures that would all have shipped invisible:

The page would have rendered in Times — Tailwind v4 tree-shook the @theme font variables, so every var(--font-mono) in my base CSS resolved to nothing. Fixed with literal stacks; re-grepped to confirm.
Every vermilion label would have been sumi — unlayered .lbl { color: inherit } beats @layer utilities text-colours. Removed.
Title art would have pushed its caption off-screen.
Plus: sea/storm draw order, an ash-wrap span too small for tall viewports, stale tail geometry across restart, duplicate col-span-2 in the 1-column rail, and a missing Canvas error boundary.

Two probe assertions were also corrected by arithmetic — most importantly, moving embers to the centre line and lulls to the cliffs, which turns "greed dies of tears" from a 40 % coin flip into a deterministic outcome, and confirming that a starved climber's post-fuel 6.03 m/s is caught at ≈1,200 m, ~200 m short of the deck.

Built the project
SALVAGE ORBIT is built, probed and shipping green.

What it is
A tether-salvage game rendered as a 1970s mission-control CRT. Grapple dead metal in a junkyard orbit, swing it on a real spring-damper tether, and release it the frame its predicted arc crosses the cyan intake ring — above 150 m/s, or the intake rejects it. Six escalating storm sectors, a quota, a moonlet in the middle of every straight line, and three honest ways to lose.

The four answers (full text in design_notebook.md)
Q1 The player improvises and ends an arc that existed once — a viewer can't re-derive the shot.
Q2 Swing captured debris into the cyan intake before the clock empties or the field punctures the hull, because every swing costs propellant and the intake rejects anything under 150 m/s.
Q3 Grapple or let pass, priced both ways and recurring every few seconds — plus a tether-length sub-decision (reach vs. velocity) that flips which side is right as sectors escalate.
Q4 Asteroids (1979) and Osmos (2009) are the neighbours; neither has a tether, inherited swing velocity, energy injection from reeling in, or a velocity-gated moving intake.
Verification — actually executed, not claimed
npm run build runs node scripts/probe.mjs first (esbuild-bundled, Node-executed). Final output:

text

PROBE OK — 19 checks, 0 failures
✓ 39 modules transformed.
dist/index.html  1,228.25 kB │ gzip: 807.88 kB
The probe went 4 → 4 → 2 → 1 → 0 failures across eight runs and found four real defects code review missed: the pilot was re-grappled its own released payload and cancelling its shots (→ 2.6 s commit lockout, now a design feature); reeling cost the entire fuel tank (0.7 → 0.06/m); ambient debris scored without the player (→ only player-released mass is refinable); and the prediction arc integrated at 1/60 while the sim stepped at 1/120 (→ PRED_DT === DT, armedMiss went 21 → 0).

Direction as built
Unlit brushed-aluminium console (#0E1317) around a black bezel (#07090C); everything on screen is a luminous stroke, never a filled block — phosphor amber #FFB000 as you, intake cyan #4DE0E8 as the goal, alarm #FF3B1F on the hull. Archivo 800 against JetBrains Mono with tabular figures everywhere; 0.22em tracked micro-caps under every readout. A fixed 302 px instrument rail owns all telemetry while the CRT bleeds right. Three AI-generated images (title plate, rail metal, refinery end plate) are inlined and all three carry onError fallbacks.

Not verified: there is no browser in this sandbox, so I never saw it run — pixels, audio and feel are audited by reading the code back, and the README says exactly that rather than implying a playtest.

Built the project
Done. I built FLOWLINE — a complete, original momentum gliding game, and verified it headlessly.

What shipped
Pure simulation (src/game/): fixed-step (1/120s), deterministic, seeded — no Math.random/Math.random in sim code, no top-level side effects. A readable analytic flow field (flowAt) is the single source of truth for both the physics and the on-screen current.
Renderer (src/render.ts): a Canvas-2D painter's stack — abyss sky → parallax stars → advected flow streaks → miasma → shaded rocks with drop shadows → glowing nodes → portal → luminous hero with heat-tinted glow trail + squash/stretch → vignette. Cool key "current", warm hero glow that shifts cyan→orange with heat.
Audio (src/audio.ts): fully procedural WebAudio (ambient pad, thrust noise loop, collect/overheat/death/win SFX). Mute drops master gain within a frame; pause suspends the context.
App (src/App.tsx): title (with living attract-mode background), HUD (score/nodes/Light/Heat meters), pause, mute, restart, level-complete, death, and "all currents mastered" screens. Mouse and keyboard control, resize/blur-safe, corrupt-localStorage guarded, no white-flash.
The game (why it's a game, not a toy)
You ride a luminous seed through a living current, collecting nodes to open the gate. The recurring decision — thrust now (spend heat) vs. ride the flow (conserve heat) — has real costs on both sides: over-thrust → overheat lockout that strands you in a deadly current; under-thrust → you drift into the dark. Failure is spatial, not a clock.

Verification (actually executed)
The probe (scripts/probe.mjs → esbuild → node) runs the real sim through naive/greedy/idle policies and is wired into the prebuild hook, so a broken game fails the build loudly. 17/17 green: all 4 levels winnable, greed and timidity both fail (two distinct loss causes), deterministic, numerically stable, geometry fair, restart resets, first goal reachable in <8s. Then vite build produced a single self-contained dist/index.html (offline, no network).

Honest limitation
This sandbox has no browser, so I could not visually play-test the pixels/audio/feel — I verified the render/audio code by construction and tuned physics against the probe's policy. That's disclosed in the README alongside the full ENV, PREMISE_NOTE, design pillars, director statement, Q1–Q3 answers, and fun line.

Run it with npm run build && npm run preview.

MURMURATION is built and shipping clean. Here's what I made and what I honestly know about it.

The game
You are a falconer's hawk over a river valley at dusk. Three hundred starlings will not follow you — they only flee you. Move the hawk and the murmuration deforms around it; that's your only verb. Push the flock 2.9 km east to the roost wood before the storm front rolls over the valley, losing as few birds as you can to four named causes: wires, falcon, ground, front.

The recurring decision: push on, or pull together? Shoving (hold click to flare) gains ground on the front but shears stragglers off the cloud — and a lone bird is exactly what a peregrine stoops for. Rallying (space, 6.5 s cooldown) balls the flock up so the falcon aborts, but costs ~40 % of your speed for 2.4 s, which the front charges you for. The same trade recurs vertically at every wire gate: height is free tailwind and falcon country; under the wires is slow, tight and safe.

Architecture
game/ — fixed 60 Hz sim in structure-of-arrays Float32Arrays: boids with topological 7-neighbour flocking (Ballerini et al. 2008), grid-accelerated k-NN, no per-frame allocation, seeded RNG only, zero DOM imports. The route is derived from the heightfield (ground(x) + driftAgl(x) vs hazardTopNear(x) + 30), so level clearance holds by construction.
render/ — hand-written 2-D painter's stack obeyed in order: sky → sun + 16 rotating god-rays → parallax clouds → 3 hill planes → ground, river and glitter → trees → wire gates → storm wall → flock (4-frame flap sprites, composited as shadow/body/additive trail/additive warm rim) → falcons → hawk → particles → grain, haze, vignette. One motivated key light that dies as the run progresses; dusk→night palette lerp is the progress bar.
ui/ — React shell: fixed-step accumulator, input clamped to the visible frame each frame, pause/mute/restart, HUD, title, graded results.
Verification — read this part
Executed: npm run build — clean, TypeScript-clean, single-file dist/index.html (537 kB, image inlined via ?inline).
Not executed: the probe (src/game/probe.ts, 11 assertions: determinism, naive win, greedy fails, timid gets caught, ≥3 loss causes, no dead state, route clearance, restart, hawk in frame). This sandbox exposes no shell — install_npm_packages rejects file:/./ paths, so the package-manager route to run it was attempted and failed. I did not see it pass, and the README says so plainly. Balance figures are derived on paper, not measured.
I cannot view images, so the one generated dusk plate is used only as a blurred, darkened title backdrop behind the live flock, with a procedural sky as fallback.
Bugs found and fixed by static audit: hand-placed route altitudes collided with real terrain (replaced with the derived generator); the cohesion metric sampled random birds instead of nearest neighbours (would have triggered permanent falcon stoops); falcon cadence was a death spiral; the storm was retuned twice into a front that builds 18.5 → 22.5 m/s.
If the flock's boids weights don't read as a legible cloud on first play, every dial is in src/game/config.ts — W_COH, STORM_SPEED_0/1 and FALCON_REGROUP.

I built WAGGLE, a 3D game where you play a scout honeybee and the waggle dance is the controls. The final build succeeds as one offline file (dist/index.html, about 1.6 MB), and a gameplay probe that runs inside every build passes all 16 checks. I never saw it running: there's no browser here, so the 3D scene, shaders, audio and frame rate are built to spec but unseen.

The game: you fly over a September meadow, sip flower patches, fly home and dance. You press, drag and hold on the honeycomb: the direction from the centre is the angle from the sun, and the hold time is the distance (1 s = 400 m). Five simulated foragers per dance circuit decode that and fly where it points, so a shaky or mistimed dance sends them to empty grass. You have four days to store 18 kg of honey.

The camera always faces the sun, so "up" on screen and "up" on the comb mean the same thing: you dance what you saw. The sun is a real sun for September in southern England.

The recurring decision is whether to dance now for the near, small patches or scout farther for big ones. Scouting farther costs idle time, longer forager trips and bigger misses. The richest ivy grows where hornets hunt, and the more bees you send there, the more hornets take.

What the probe caught: it plays the real rules with seven scripted players on five meadows, and the early builds failed on real design problems:

An all-in greedy player could never wipe out the colony, so that loss path didn't exist.
Day 4 barely produced honey for a first-timer.
The hornet ivy was a trap: even sensible use cost 21 bees and earned less than avoiding it, so it wasn't a real choice.
I fixed these by making hornet danger rise with how many bees you send, moving the colony-collapse line to 26 bees, and warming day 4. After that:

The average player wins every seed with 1–1.8 kg to spare.
Always dancing for the nearest patch starves, and scouting everything first wins only 1 time in 5.
Using the ivy moderately earns more honey but costs about 11 bees; sending everyone there collapses the colony on 3 of 5 seeds.
Random play loses, doing nothing still ends the game, runs are deterministic, restart resets, and a dance in the opposite direction lands zero recruits.
Environment: I could install packages and run the build, but had no shell and could not edit package.json or the Vite config. So the probe runs from postcss.config.mjs, which Vite loads during the build; a failed check fails the build. It adds nothing to the bundle.

Main risks:

Performance: 36,000 grass tufts plus bloom may be heavy on low-end GPUs. Settings → Plain halves the grass and drops the effects.
Fallbacks: if WebGL fails or the 3D view crashes, the game switches to a 2D map view with the same rules; the effects layer falls back to plain rendering.
Not play-tested by a person: the feel of the drag-and-hold dance with a real mouse, the day-one hints, and a full 10–12 minute season.
Images: I generated two (title art and a winter end screen) and checked both for baked-in text; neither has any. Everything else — textures, the straw hive, trees, grass, the honeycomb shader, sky and sound — is procedural code.

README.md has the four design answers, the full probe output, receipts and an honest self-assessment; design_notebook.md has the two candidate premises, real-world numbers and module layout. The code is in src/game/ (rules and probe), src/render/, src/audio/, src/app/ and src/ui/.

The probe (headless, pure sim):

Piece 1's first goal is reachable by a "naive" policy: tap at the exact target tempo (zero jitter), Y = the curve value at that time, cue when told → assert: finished, no collapse, medal ≥ bronze. (This also proves the win is reachable.)
Greed fails: Y always at 100 (fff), ignore the band, tap evenly but at wrong tempo (always fast) → assert: collapse or fail (tempo/life low → fail the medal).
Timidity fails: never tap (the band wanders) → assert: collapse (smear) or fail.
No dead state: run each piece to completion under a scripted policy; assert state is 'finished' or 'collapsed' within the piece length + epsilon; assert restart resets (same piece, same seed → identical state after N steps of the same input script → deterministic).
Reachable with unlocked mechanics: no locks (all pieces selectable; each piece's required mechanics exist from the start) — assert: pieces 3 (rubato) and 4 (soloist) can be won by a policy using only tap + Y + Space.
Control mapping: the sim exposes the tempo response: tapping faster than target raises the ensemble tempo (monotonic check), Y maps monotonically to dynamics.
Every level beatable with that level's tools: covered by 5.

OK, now the score/music generation. I need pieces that sound good. Design:

Style parameters: key (root midi, scale), bpm, time-signature feel (4/4 or 3/4 for the waltz), a chord-progression template (an array of degrees per bar, e.g. I–V–vi–IV in major; i–VI–III–VII in minor), a voice list: count and instrument and role (melody / harmony / bass / counter / percussion).
Melody: step over beats: from a scale, pick a note (a random walk seeded with a contour template, e.g. [0,1,2,4,5,4,2,1] degrees offset), a rhythm pattern (quarter, eighth pair, half), a phrase = 8 beats ending on the tonic (a downbeat resolution rule).
Harmony: arpeggiate the chord (root position, 8th notes or quarter), a different octave.
Bass: the chord's root on beat 1, the 5th on 3 (4/4) or beat 3 (3/4), octave 2–3, a longer duration.
Counter (if ≥6 voices): a 3rd above the melody, dotted.
Percussion: soft pulse: kick on 1&3? A soft noise "shaker" on the eighths at low vel, a snare-ish on 2&4 in the march/carnival. Keep it gentle.
MIDI→freq: 440×2^((m−69)/12).
Envelope: the per-note gain envelope (an attack 10–40ms, a decay, a release) × the voice gain × the global dynamics (read at schedule time) — the player's Y controls the global gain: audible response to the gesture within ~50ms.
The waltz (3/4): the melody rhythm in 3/4; the tap = quarter-note tempo 108 (0.556s/beat — fine).

Volume/harshness: master 0.55 → compressor (threshold −18dB, ratio 3) → destination; per-voice gain ~0.12; overall safe. A "warmth": a gentle low-pass on the master (8k) to kill the digital edge.

Now the checks design (shared, headless):

ts


export interface CheckResult { check: string; ok: boolean; detail?: string }
export function runChecks(): { results: CheckResult[]; fails: number }
Policies: a "conductor" object with functions called by the harness: onStep(t, sim) → may call sim.tap(), sim.setY(v), sim.cue(). Harness: create the sim for the piece; a count-in phase: the sim handles the count-in internally (phase 'countin' 4 beats at the target bpm; the piece starts at grid=0). Simpler: the sim starts at t=0 in 'countin', duration 4 beats at the piece's base bpm (with a tick for the audio); at the end of the count-in → 'playing'. Input during count-in is allowed (taps set the tempo; Y is recorded; no grade).

Checks:

c1_first_goal: piece 1, human-ish policy (tap at the target with 12ms jitter seeded, Y = the curve clamped with a lag of 0.05, no cue) → assert: finished (not collapsed), overall ≥ 45 (bronze).
c2_perfect: piece 1, oracle policy (exact tempo, exact curve Y) → assert: gold (≥82). (Ceiling reachable.)
c3_greed_fails: piece 1, tap at 1.5× the tempo + Y = 1.0 always → assert: result is not gold — specifically collapse or overall < 45 (greed fails).
c4_timidity_fails: piece 1, no taps, Y at mid → assert: collapse (band wanders) [or fail].
c5_no_dead_state: all 4 pieces, oracle policy (tempo exact including the rubato curve, Y exact, cues at window center) → each: finished with bronze or above (every level beatable with unlocked tools: oracle uses only tap/Y/cue).
c6_end_bounded: assert each run ends in ≤ piece length + 10 seconds (no infinite state).
c7_determinism: piece 2, fixed policy (scripted input), run twice with the same seed → identical final grade + musician state (serialized).
c8_restart: after a collapse, create a new sim with the same pieceId → state equal to a fresh one (offset, etc.).
c9_control_mapping: piece 1: tap at 1.25× the target for 8 beats → ensembleBpm > target; tap at 0.8× → < target (monotonic); setY(0) → dynamics < setY(1) (monotonic).
c10_collapse_cause: (covered by 3/4, but assert the collapse cause is reported: the sim has a lastCause 'smear' | 'none').
c11_solo_mechanic: piece 4 oracle with a cue vs without a cue → the with-cue life grade is higher (the cue works).
A run of a 40–70-second piece at 60Hz = ~2500–4200 steps × ~12 policies → trivial compute.

Now let me also make sure the sim API is clean for the probe:

ts


export type PieceId = 'overture' | 'waltz' | 'procession' | 'carnival';
export function getPiece(id): PieceDef  // static config including musicians, bpmCurve(beats)->bpm, phrase(beats)->dyn(0..1), bandTol, cueBeats[]
export function buildScore(pieceId): Score // seeded note events (cached)
export function createSim(pieceId, seed?): Sim
sim: { t, phase: 'countin'|'playing'|'finished'|'collapsed', gridBeat, bpm, tapTempo, jitter, clarity, y, dynamics, musicians: Musician[] (fixed array, mutated), smear, tempoErr, life (accumulated), grades {sync, tempo, life}, cause, endedBeat, lengthBeats }
export function tap(sim), setY(sim, v), cuePress(sim)
export function step(sim, dt)
The sim also tracks: count-in beats; after the count-in, grade integration: sync = 100×(1 − Σsmear dt / T), etc.

Musician update (per step):



m.personalBpm = sim.bpm * (1 + m.bias(t))  // bias may oscillate
m.offset += (m.personalBpm - sim.bpm) / sim.bpm * dt_beats  // dt in beats: dt * (personalBpm/bpm − 1)… note: offset in beats = ∫(fpb − f)dt, f is in beats/sec.
Correction: m.offset *= exp(−clarity × m.attention × k × dt)  (exponential decay toward 0)
m.offset wrapped to (−0.5, 0.5]
m.smear = clamp((|m.offset| − win) / (0.5 − win))
Wait — the offset dynamics: personal frequency vs grid frequency: d(offset)/dt = (fpb − f_grid). If bias is +2% and bpm is 90 (1.5 bps): 0.03 bps → 30 beats (20s) to reach 0.6 beats. Too slow to feel? With a correction term, the equilibrium offset = drift rate / correction rate. Set the correction k so the equilibrium is meaningful: with clarity 1 (perfect tap), the equilibrium offset ≈ a tiny value; with clarity 0.3 (sloppy tap) + bias 3%: equilibrium = (0.03 bps) / (0.3×k). If k = 0.15 /s → 0.03/0.045 = 0.66 beats → fully smeared. If k = 0.5 → 0.2 beats → mild smear. Nice tuning knob. The smear window = 0.10 beats. Let me define: correctionRate = 0.55 × clarity × m.attention (per second). At piece 4, bias 5% at 128bpm (2.13 bps): 0.107 bps drift; clarity 1.0 → equilibrium 0.19 beats (smeary — must sustain perfect evenness; a dip in evenness → the offset accumulates until it recovers). Hmm, that might be too hard for the troublemaker; the troublemaker's bias oscillates: it swings away then comes back (sin) — you can also ride it (the offset naturally returns). Fine; the oracle in the checks is clarity = 1 → equilibrium 0.19 → the troublemaker alone has smear = (0.19−0.10)/0.4 = 0.225 → the ensemble's (1 of 8) average = 0.028 → no collapse, sync slightly dented. Good — the troublemaker is annoying, not fatal; the fatality is the player's sloppy taps.

Clarity definition: clarity = clamp01(1 − jitterNorm) × clamp01(1 − |tapTempo − targetBpm|/15), where jitterNorm = std/mean of the last 5 tap intervals. While taps are recent (< 1.2s), clarity is high. No taps → clarity decays to 0 (the band wanders freely) → c4 fails as expected.

Tap tempo: an EMA of intervals (the last 4). At the start (few taps), the ensemble holds the piece's base bpm.

Ensemble bpm: when a tap arrives (and the tap tempo is valid), sim.bpm = lerp(sim.bpm, tapTempo, 0.25); decay: sim.bpm drifts slightly toward the musicians' average bias: sim.bpm += avgBias × 0.02 × dt? Keep it small.

The target bpm curve for the rubato (piece 3): bpmTarget(b) = 76 → 60 over beats 24–40 (smooth). tempoErr = |sim.bpm − bpmTarget(grid)|; the tempo grade = 100×(1 − mean(err/12)) clamped.

The life grade: 100 × fraction of time |dynamics − curve| ≤ tol (0.28? a per-piece tolerance: piece 1 0.30, later 0.22). dynamics = the player's Y (a smoothed EMA of setY, tau 0.15s) — the baton's height = the volume (the actual master gain of the ensemble audio also follows Y! so Y is audibly meaningful).

The sync grade: 100×(1 − meanSmear), meanSmear = time-averaged ensembleSmear, where ensembleSmear = max? mean? use a blend: 0.5×mean + 0.5×max (a single lost player hurts).

Overall = 0.35×sync + 0.30×tempo + 0.35×life (weights; the piece card shows the three bars). Pass = overall ≥ 45 and no collapse. Medals: bronze ≥ 45, silver ≥ 65, gold ≥ 82.

Collapse: ensembleSmearSustained: track a timer: while meanSmear > 0.62 → timer += dt, else timer = max(0, timer − dt×2); ≥ 1.2s → collapse, cause 'smear'. Also a hard collapse: if |tempoErr| > 25 bpm for more than 2s, cause 'tempo' (you dragged the band off the map entirely) — a second failure cause (the "two or more failure causes" ✓: smear collapse, tempo collapse, plus a grade fail (finished but under 45), plus a missed cue (only the life penalty, not fatal). Good.

Count-in: 4 beats at the base bpm; the sim exposes countBeat for the HUD/audio tick; the musicians' offset is seeded at ±0.02.

The soloist: piece definition solo: { musicianIndex, entryBeat, windowStart, windowEnd } (in beats, the window before the entry? Let's say the window [entry−1.2, entry−0.2]). On cuePress: if in the window → m.cued = true (the soloist plays their line, +10 life bonus, a flash); if missed by the entry beat → the soloist's gain = 0.35 (a muted, lost) & a life −12 (a one-time penalty), visual a slouch. If cued late (after the window, before the entry? the window is only before the entry; press after the entry → nothing (a small "late" flash, no bonus, no penalty? Let's say: late cue = no bonus, the soloist plays normally). Simplify: cued in the window → bonus; else → no bonus, no penalty. And the check c11: with-cue life > without-cue ✓.

The soloist music: their line is a melody variation at the entry — in the score generation, the soloist's part starts at the entryBeat with a distinctive rhythm. Without a cue: their notes are played at low velocity (0.3) — an audible difference.

Q1 — Why must it be played?: "The player is the pulse that eight simulated musicians follow; their bow-arm evenness, their tap tempo, and the baton's height literally move, lock, and swell the sound. A viewer of a recording sees a band; they can't feel the moment the drift comes back to zero under their gesture — the artifact is a performance that exists only while you conduct."

Q2 — "Keep the baton even to lock the band to the pulse, hold the baton height to the phrase the score demands, and the piece is done; the band drifts apart if your tempo wavers, or the judges call it flat if you're afraid of the swell — and the fun is feeling an eight-player ensemble tighten around your hand and hearing the piece come alive."

Q3 — "Every phrase: a swell is demanded while a section drifts. Tighten your gesture and relock the band, and the swell goes flat and the 'life' score drops; commit to the swell, and the drift deepens toward the smear point where the piece collapses. Neither is always right: always safe = a dead performance (fails on life), always bold = the band falls apart (a collapse)."

Q4 — "Closest shipped: Guitar Hero / Rock Band (you play an instrument against a scrolling note chart) and the toy 'Conduct' app (no goal, no agent). The podium's difference: you don't play an instrument — you direct other agents who each have their own tempo bias and drift; the input is gesture timing (tap evenness + height), not note-hitting; the win is a graded performance by the simulated ensemble, not a combo score."

Premise candidates (notebook): (1) "The Last Cut" — edit a 10-shot short film; the audience simulation reacts; a creative family. (2) The podium (this). Why The podium: the minute-1 fun is immediate and auditory; the decision is physical and recurring; the audio is the reward itself.

Neither falls under the threat / meter / rationing umbrella — the pressure is skill against a simulated ensemble, not an advancing threat. I shipped The podium, because its minute-1 loop (tap the pulse, watch the band lock in, hear the swell) is legible and audible in the first 60 seconds."

The Y input mapping: Y is the baton height: pointer y from the top of the stage area; dyn = clamp((stageBottomPx − y)/span). The stage area: y from the h×0.30 (the top of the band area) to the h×0.86 (the podium). If the pointer is above → 1 (fff), below → 0 (ppp). On desktop, the hover also sets Y (a continuous baton), a tap = click. On touch: Y = the touch position on pointerdown/move.

The dynamics smoothing: sim.dyn = lerp toward y with tau 0.12s: dyn += (y − dyn)×(1 − exp(−dt/0.12)).

The audio ensemble gain = 0.5 (the master) × (0.12 + 0.88×dyn^1.25) × 0.9 (the piece level) — during count-in ×0.5. A note vel factor.

Master chain: ensembleGain → masterGain (0.55 or muted 0) → lowpass 7.5k → compressor → destination. The applause goes through masterGain too (a separate gain node).

rng.ts
ts


export function mulberry32(seed: number): () => number {
  let a = seed >>> 0;
  return function () {
    a |= 0; a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) | 0;
    let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
    t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
}
export function hashStr(s: string): number {
  let h = 2166136261 >>> 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) { h ^= s.charCodeAt(i); h = Math.imul(h, 16777619); }
  return h >>> 0;
}

ts


import { mulberry32, hashStr } from './rng';
export type PieceId = 'overture' | 'waltz' | 'procession' | 'carnival';
export type Instrument = 'violin' | 'viola' | 'cello' | 'oboe' | 'flute' | 'clarinet' | 'brass' | 'harp' | 'drums';
export interface MusicianDef {
  instrument: Instrument;
  bias: number;      // tempo bias as a fraction (+ fast / − slow)
  wobble: number;    // wobble amplitude (fraction, 0 = none)
  wobblePeriod: number; // seconds
  wobblePhase: number;
  attention: number; // how strongly pulled to the conductor (0..1)
  hair: number;      // visual variant 0..2
}
export interface SoloDef { voice: number; entryBeat: number; windowStart: number; windowEnd: number; }
export interface PieceDef {
  id: PieceId; no: number; title: string; subtitle: string; key: string;
  baseBpm: number; beats: number; timeSig: [number, number];
  bandTol: number;
  musicians: MusicianDef[];
  solo?: SoloDef;
  bpmAt: (b: number) => number;
  phraseAt: (b: number) => number;
  difficulty: 1|2|3|4;
}
Melody: per piece, an array of arrays: mel: number[][] (degrees from the root, 0=root of the melody octave). And a chord progression: prog: number[][], each chord = array of scale degrees (midi offset relative to the root).

Write a builder:

ts


interface ScoreSpec {
  root: number;        // midi root (e.g., A2 for bass reference)
  scale: number[];     // semitone intervals
  bpm..., prog: (number[] | null)[]; // per bar: degrees
  melBase: number;     // midi = root4? use a melBase midi for degree 0
  mel: (number | [number, number])[][]; // per bar per beat: degree or [degree, durBeats]
  waltz?: boolean;     // 3/4
  percStyle?: 'none'|'soft'|'march';
}
Notes per voice:

voice 0 melody: for each bar, beat k (0..barLen-1): degree → midi = melBase + deg2semi(scale, deg); dur default 0.9 (or given), vel 0.9.
harmony voice: 8th-note arpeggio: for each 0.5 beat: pattern [0, 7, 12, 7] scale degrees +12 above the root? Use chord degrees: chord = [d0, d1, d2] (triad); arp degrees = [d0+12, d1+12, d0+24, d1+12]; midi = root3 + scaleSemi. vel 0.55. dur 0.45.
bass voice: beat 0: root +0? midi root1 (low): dur barLen-0.2? dur 1.8, vel 0.8; beat 2: 5th (+7 semitone via scale degree d1), dur 1.8, vel 0.7. (In waltz: beat 0 root, beat 2 5th.)
counter voice (if present): sustain on beat 0 with a chord tone (d2+12), dur 3.8, vel 0.5; plus beat 2.5? keep it simple, sustain only.
perc voice (if drums): march: tom on beat 0 (kind 'noise', midi -1 → use midi 40 with kind 'noise' + freq hint? encode midi -1 for noise-low (tom), -2 for noise-high (shaker), -3 for snare (mid)). For march: tom on beats 0 and 2? classic: snare on 2&4 → beats 2 (0-indexed: 1,3) of the 4-beat bar; shaker 8ths at vel 0.15; tom 0 vel 0.6. soft (waltz/procession): shaker on every beat at vel 0.12? or soft brush: noise-low at beats 0,2 vel 0.2.
Chord degrees → midi: chord root = scale degree: chord midi = rootMidi3 (e.g., for A major: A3=57; define root3 per piece) + scaleSemi(deg % 12), + 12×(deg/12 | 0) scale-octave handling. Let's define helper deg2semi(scale, deg): scale length 7; octave = floor(deg/7); pos = deg mod 7; semi = scale[pos] + 12*octave.

Melody is degrees relative to melBase midi (deg 0 = melBase). melBase = root4 (e.g., A4=69). Degrees can be negative (below the base).

import { getPieces, PieceId, PieceDef, buildScore, Score } from './score';
import { mulberry32, hashStr } from './rng';
export type Phase = 'countin' | 'playing' | 'finished' | 'collapsed';
export interface MusicianState {
  offset: number; smear: number; cued: boolean; biasPhase: number;
}
export interface Grades { sync: number; tempo: number; life: number; overall: number; medal: number; }
export interface Sim {
  id: number;
  piece: PieceDef; score: Score;
  phase: Phase; t: number; grid: number; bpm: number;
  tapTimes: number[]; tapCount: number; tapTempo: number; jitter: number; clarity: number; lastTapT: number;
  y: number; dyn: number;
  musicians: MusicianState[];
  grip: number; smearHold: number; tempoHold: number;
  meanErr: number; // running mean bpm error
  accGrip: number; accErr: number; accInside: number; // beats
  soloCued: boolean; soloMissed: boolean;
  grades: Grades; cause: 'smear' | 'tempo' | 'none';
  endReason: 'none' | 'finished' | 'collapsed';
  pulses: number; // tap pulse counter (for fx)
  countPulse: number; // count-in tick counter
}
let simSeq = 1;
export const COUNT_BEATS = 4;
export function createSim(pieceId: PieceId): Sim { ... }
export function tap(sim: Sim): void
export function setY(sim: Sim, v: number): void
export function cue(sim: Sim): void
export function step(sim: Sim, dt: number): void
export function liveGrades(sim): Grades  (running)
Wait — live grades: the HUD wants a running average; compute in liveGrades(sim) from the accumulators / elapsed beats. Final grades stored on end.

createSim: rng = mulberry32(hashStr(pieceId)); offset init: (rng()−0.5)×0.06; biasPhase rng()×2π.

tap: if phase is not countin/playing return; t = sim.t; if tapCount>0: interval = t − lastTapT; if 0.15 < interval < 1.5: push to ring buffer (last 5): tapTimes[head++ %5], count++. mean, std → jitter = std/mean; tapTempo = 60/mean; sim.bpm += (clamp(tapTempo, 40, 220) − sim.bpm) × 0.35; lastTapT = t; pulses++.

clarity (computed in step): if tapCount<2 → 0; fresh = lastTapT within 1.2s: recency = clamp01(1 − (t − lastTapT)/1.2); tempoAcc = clamp01(1 − |tapTempo − targetBpm|/15); clarity = (1 − clamp01(jitter/0.25)) × tempoAcc × recency. (jitter 0.15 → 0.4; 0.03 → 0.88.)

step:

if phase is finished/collapsed: t += dt (for anim); musicians keep drifting slightly? freeze musicians (cleaner): musicians frozen, dyn decays to 0.1? just t += dt, and return.
t += dt.
y smoothing: dyn += (y − dyn) × (1 − exp(−dt/0.12)).
if phase 'countin': grid += baseBpm/60×dt; countTick = when floor(−grid) changes → countPulse++ (audio + fx). When grid ≥ 0: grid = 0; phase 'playing'; bpm = clamp(tapTempo valid ? tapTempo : baseBpm, base×0.8, base×1.25).
if 'playing': grid += bpm/60×dt; update clarity (as above); update each musician: biasFrac = def.bias + wobble×sin(2π t/period + phase); offset += (bpm/60) × biasFrac × dt; correction: off *= exp(−0.5 × clarity × att × dt); wrap; smear = clamp01((|off|−0.08)/0.32).
grip = 0.5×(mean + max) of smear.
solo: if solo && !soloCued && !soloMissed: if grid > windowEnd && grid <= entry: (missed only when entry passes) if grid >= entry && !cued: if no cue → soloMissed = true (apply penalty at the end; soloist goes muted). If cue(): if within window → cued (soloCued=true), if not (after entry): late → no bonus, no penalty (soloist plays normally, just no bonus: soloCued=false, soloMissed=false → "late").
Accumulate (only when grid is in [0,L]): dtBeats = bpm/60×dt: accGrip += grip×dtBeats; err = |bpm − bpmAt(min(grid,L))|; accErr += err×dtBeats; inside = |dyn − phraseAt(grid)| ≤ bandTol → accInside += dtBeats (else 0).
bpm drift: average musicians' bias: sim.bpm += avgBiasFrac×bpm×0.03×dt (small wander when player is passive).
bpm smoothing handled by taps.
collapse: if grip > 0.5: smearHold += dt, else smearHold = max(0, smearHold − dt×1.5); if ≥ 1.4 → collapsed('smear'). tempo: if err > 22: tempoHold += dt, else decay; ≥ 2.5 → collapsed('tempo').
finish: if grid ≥ L → finished; compute final grades; medal.
On collapsed/finished: compute grades (final).*
Compute grades(g): T = L: sync = 100×clamp01(1 − accGrip/L); tempo = 100×clamp01(1 − (accErr/L)/20); life = 100×(accInside/L); if solo: if soloCued life += 8, else if soloMissed life −= 12; clamp. overall = .35s+.30t+.35l. medal: collapsed → 0; overall ≥ 90 → 3; ≥68 → 2; ≥45 → 1; else 0.

Hmm wait — oracle tempo check: oracle taps exactly bpmAt(grid) each beat; but tapTempo = 60/mean(intervals); intervals in time = 60/bpmTarget → tapTempo = bpmTarget ✓; sim.bpm lerps 0.35 per tap → lag ~2-3 bpm → meanErr ~2 → tempo ≈ 90 ✓.

But a subtlety: in rubato, target changes slowly; the lerp tracks ✓.

Also note: tap interval measured in sim seconds; grid-based policies tap in time at the current target rate ✓.

cue(sim): if phase playing && solo: w = solo; if !soloCued: if grid ≥ w.windowStart && grid ≤ w.windowEnd → soloCued = true; (else nothing (early or late)); also if grid > w.entry && !soloMissed → do nothing (late, no penalty).

Musician cued flag for soloist: musicians[solo.voice].cued = soloCued (used for audio vel and render highlight).

liveGrades(sim): elapsed = clamp(grid, 0, L); if elapsed <= 0 return {all 100? or 0} → return 100s (nothing yet). Otherwise same formula with acc/elapsed.

Harness:

ts


function run(pieceId, policy, maxT): Sim {
  const sim = createSim(pieceId);
  let t = 0; const dt = 1/60;
  policy.begin(sim);
  let guard = 0;
  while ((sim.phase === 'countin' || sim.phase === 'playing') && guard < 20000) {
    policy.act(sim);
    step(sim, dt); t += dt; guard++;
  }
  return sim;
}
Policies (each constructed with a seed):

oracle(piece): act: target = piece.bpmAt(clamp(grid,0,L)); if (t ≥ nextTap) { tap; nextTap = t + 60/target; } setY(clamp(phraseAt(grid),0,1)); if solo && !cued && grid in window → cue. begin: nextTap = 0 (first tap at t=0? count-in starts t=0 → tap immediately ✓). Note: oracle uses target time interval from current t — with a changing bpm, intervals adapt ✓ (jitter ~0 since intervals are computed from the constant target at each tap; small drift → small jitter ✓).
casual: taps at fixed 60/92 interval + jitter (rng ±14ms), setY(phrase −0.05 clamp), no cue.
greed: taps at 60/138, y=1.
timidity: y=0.5, no taps.
blackout: 12 beats oracle, then for 3 beats no taps (y holds), then resume.
determinism policy: taps on a fixed time script (e.g., every 0.7s), y = 0.5 + 0.4×sin(t) — no need for seeded rng (deterministic) → run twice, compare serialized {grades, offsets×4, grid, bpm} with strict equality? Floating-point determinism: same operations → identical bits ✓.

private playTone(mus: VoiceChain, when, dur, midi, vel, cents, kind: Instrument) {
  const f = 440 × 2^((midi−69)/12);
  switch:
  strings (violin/viola/cello): 2 osc saw, detune ±6 + cents, lp freq (violin 2600, viola 2000, cello 1300) + vel×300, gain env: attack 0.015+0.02, sustain vel×0.5, release: total dur: env: g.gain: 0→peak (0.5×vel×0.5?) peak 0.22×vel... per-voice balance: strings 0.30, winds 0.26, brass 0.30, harp 0.26, drums 0.5.
  oboe: osc saw + osc triangle (×0.6), lp 2400; attack 0.03 (reed).
  flute: sine ×1 + triangle 0.5, lp 3200, breath: noise gain 0.02×vel hp 3000, attack 0.04.
  clarinet: saw (lp 1500) + sine, attack 0.02.
  brass: 2 saw detune ±8, lp 2000, attack 0.04, peak 0.28×vel.
  harp: sine + sine×2 (×0.3), fast exp decay 0.5s min(dur), pluck attack 0.004.
}
Noise kind: -1 tom: osc sine 160→70 exp, 0.25s; -2 shaker: noise hp 5000 bp? gain 0.16×vel 0.05s; -3 snare: noise bp 1800 0.09s + osc 190 0.06s.

export function ghostConduct(sim: Sim): void {
  if (sim.phase === 'collapsed') return;
  const target = sim.piece.bpmAt(clamp(sim.grid, 0, L));
  const want = 60 / target;

Let's also think about how the tap tempo is initialized: before 2 taps, tapTempo = baseBpm, clarity 0 → musicians free to drift — but correction ~0 during count-in? During count-in, correction should be strong (count-in is the lock): use clarity = 1 during count-in? but player taps are few... correction rate uses clarity; during count-in set clarity = 0.8 (band watches the downbeat) so offsets settle small before playing. ✓ Also bpm during count-in stays at base.

kf helper:

ts


function kf(points: [number, number][]): (b: number) => number {
  return (b) => {
    if (b <= points[0][0]) return points[0][1];
    for (let i = 1; i < points.length; i++) {
      if (b <= points[i][0]) {
        const [b0, v0] = points[i - 1]; const [b1, v1] = points[i];
        const t = (b - b0) / (b1 - b0); const s = t * t * (3 - 2 * t);
        return v0 + (v1 - v0) * s;
      }
    }
    return points[points.length - 1][1];
  };
}
deg2semi:

ts


function deg2semi(scale: number[], deg: number): number {
  const oct = Math.floor(deg / 7);
  const pos = ((deg % 7) + 7) % 7;
  return scale[pos] + 12 * oct;
}

interface Spec {

  scale: number[];

  phrasePts: [number, number][];
  bandTol: number;
  prog: number[][]; // semitones per bar (triad)
  mel: (number | [number, number])[][]; // per bar per beat: degree | [degree, dur]
  melDur: number;
  voices: VoiceSpec[];
  musicians: { instrument: Instrument; att: number; mag: number }[]; // biases assigned by rng in def
  solo?: { voice: number; entryBeat: number; windowStart: number; windowEnd: number; line: number[] };
  perc?: 'soft' | 'march' | null;
  difficulty: number;
}
interface VoiceSpec { kind: 'melody' | 'harmony' | 'bass' | 'counter' | 'echo' | 'harp' | 'drums'; vel?: number; shift?: number; delay?: number; }
buildScore(spec, rng): returns Score with notes[voiceCount]:

melody: for each bar bi, each beat k: entry = mel[bi][k]; deg = entry[0] if array, else; dur = entry[1] if array, else spec.melDur; midi = melBase + deg2semi(scale, deg); push {beat: bi×bar + k, dur, midi, vel: 0.9}.
echo: same, midi −12, beat + delay (1), vel 0.45.
harmony: 8th arpeggio: each 0.5: pattern idx: [0, 2, 1, 2] over chord tones? arp = chord tones: chord = prog[bi] (semitones). arpMidi(j) = root3 + chord[?]: tones: [chord[0], chord[1], chord[2]+12? keep: root3+chord[0], +chord[1], +12+chord[0], +chord[1]]. j = floor(k2/1)%4 → pattern [0, 1, 2, 1] of tones: tone = [c0, c1, c0+12, c1][j]. beat = bi×bar + k2×0.5, dur 0.42, vel 0.5.
bass: 4/4: beat 0: root3−12 + chord[0], dur bar×0.95... use dur 1.8 (4/4) vel 0.85; beat 2: root3−12 + chord[1], dur 1.8, vel 0.7. waltz (bar 3): beat 0 root dur 2.6; beat 2 fifth dur 0.9.
counter: beat 0: root3 + 12 + chord[2], dur bar − 0.2, vel 0.5; (procession: same).
harp: 8ths: tone pattern [c0, c1, c2, c1] + root3+12, dur 0.4, vel 0.3, slight velocity accent k2%4==0? 0.35/0.22.
drums: march: for each bar: tom (midi −1) beat 0 dur 0.3 vel 0.55; snare (−3) beats 1 and 3 dur 0.2 vel 0.5; shaker (−2) every 0.5 dur 0.06 vel 0.14 (skip? all). soft: tom beats 0, 2 vel 0.25, shaker each beat dur 0.1 vel 0.1.
solo line: at entryBeat, k: line[k] degree: midi = melBase + deg2semi(scale, deg[k]), dur 0.85, vel 0.95. (added to the solo voice).
Sort notes per voice by beat.

Then piece defs: musicians array with bias by rng seeded with hash(id): sign alternates: bias = mag × (i % 2 === 0 ? 1 : −1)? better rng: b = mag × (rng() < 0.5 ? −1 : 1). wobble: carnival's clarinet (voice index 4): wobble 0.045 period 11 phase rng×6.28; others 0. hair = floor(rng()×3).

checks.ts:

runHarness(pieceId, policy, maxT)
policies: oracle (uses ghostConduct), casual (human-ish), greed, timidity, blackout.
12 checks.
The casual policy needs a seeded rng for jitter. Implementation:

ts


function makeCasual(seed) {
  const rng = mulberry32(seed);
  const state = { nextTap: 0, base: 60/92 };
  return {
    act(sim) {
      if (sim.phase === 'countin' || sim.phase === 'playing') {
        if (sim.t >= state.nextTap) {
          tap(sim);
          state.nextTap = sim.t + state.base * (1 + (rng()*2-1)*0.045); // ±4.5%
        }
        const g = clampBeat(sim.grid, sim.piece);
        setY(sim, clamp01(sim.piece.phraseAt(g) - 0.05));
      }
    }
  };
}
Wait, casual targets piece 1 (92bpm). base=60/92 fixed ✓.

greed: nextTap interval 60/138, y=1. timidity: y=0.5, no taps. blackout: oracle for the first ~12 beats, then no taps for 3 beats (y held), then oracle resumes. State {nextTap, blackout: false, resumeAt}. det: taps every 0.7 sec, y = 0.5+0.4 sin(t×0.8).

Policy interface: act(sim: Sim).

Harness:

ts


function run(pieceId: PieceId, act: (sim: Sim) => void, maxT = 240): Sim {
  const sim = createSim(pieceId);
  const dt = 1/60;
  for (let i = 0; i < 60*maxT && (sim.phase === 'countin' || sim.phase === 'playing'); i++) {
    act(sim);
    step(sim, dt);
  }
  return sim;
}
Checks:

c01 piece1 casual: sim.phase==='finished' && grades.medal >= 1 && overall>=45.
c02 piece1 oracle: medal === 3.
c03 piece1 greed: phase==='collapsed' && cause==='tempo'.

Now for audio.ts — WebAudio ensemble engine. Key design:

Lazy initialization on user gesture (guarded try/catch).
Master chain: masterGain → lowpass(7500) → compressor → destination.
Ensemble gain → master.
Per (sim, voice): a GainNode per musician + per-instrument lowpass; keyed by sim.id.
Scheduler inside tick(sim): 25ms interval driven from the GameView's rAF? More simply: call audio.tick(sim) from the game loop's rAF (60fps = 16ms, plenty of scheduling headroom at 0.15s).
Track scheduled pointers per sim: reset on new sim.id.
Sounds: count tick, applause, collapse, UI, medal.
Mute: masterGain.gain.value = 0 immediately. Volume: setTargetAtTime.
suspend/resume on pause.
Per-instrument synth functions. Noise buffer is cached.

Watch out for TS: WebkitAudioContext typing — use (window as any).webkitAudioContext.

Note scheduling: per voice v, notes = sim.score.notes[v]; ptr[v] is the next index; lookahead = 1.2 beats. when = now + (note.beat − grid) × 60/bpm + offset×60/bpm. Guarantee when ≥ now + 0.01. dur = note.dur × 60/bpm.

Soloist muted: if piece.solo && v === solo.voice && !sim.soloCued → vel × 0.35 (lost/muted playing). Also if already cued → full.

Smear: vel × (1 − 0.35×smear); cents = clamp(offset×500, −55, 55) + per-instrument base detune.

Per-musician gain: set every tick: musGain.gain.setTargetAtTime(perInstLevel × (solo muted?0.4:1), t, 0.05)? Per-instrument level is inside the note's velocity; musician's gain is 1.0, and dynamics is handled by the ensemble gain. More simply: musician's node = just a lowpass filter + a gain(1). Per-note envelope goes to the musician's filter. Ensemble gain = master volume curve.

Envelope: per note: gain node: t: 0 → peak (attack), then decay to sustain → release at t+dur. Use linearRamp + setTarget. Keep it simple: peak = vel × level(instrument) attack: strings 0.02+0.03, wind 0.04, harp 0.004, brass 0.03, perc handled by noise. g.gain.setValueAtTime(0.0001, when); linearRampToValueAtTime(peak, when+attack); setTargetAtTime(peak×0.6, when+attack, Math.max(0.05, dur×0.25)); setTargetAtTime(0.0001, when+dur, 0.05); stop(when+dur+0.3).

Oscillators:

strings: two sawtooth waves detuned by ±7 cents; lp filter at freq violin 2800/viola 2200/cello 1400 (+vel×400); level 0.16.
oboe: saw (lp 2600) + triangle (0.5); level 0.15.
flute: sine + triangle 0.6 (lp 3600); breath noise small; level 0.14.
clarinet: saw (lp 1600) + sine 0.4; level 0.15.
brass: two saws detuned ±9, lp 2200; level 0.17.
harp: sine + sine×2.01 (0.25); fast decay setTarget(0.02); level 0.16.
drums: noise-based.
midi→freq: 440×2^((m−69)/12).

Percussion:

tom (−1): sine 150→70 exponential, 0.28s, level 0.5.
shaker (−2): noise hp 6000, 0.05s, level 0.5 (velocity already low).
snare (−3): noise bp 1800 Q1 0.09s × 0.6 + sine 180 0.06 × 0.4.
Count tick: woodblock: sine 1100 × 0.035 decay, gain 0.22; downbeat: + sine 140 × 0.06 gain 0.3.

Applause(strength 0..1): noise buffer 3.2s bp 1400 Q0.6 gain envelope: 0.05→0.5×s (0.35s)→0.1×s (1.2s)→0 (2.6s); plus claps: 26 claps at random t in 0..2.4: noise 0.03 hp 1000 gain 0.08+rand×0.3.

Collapse: saws 98, 102, 112 Hz lp 500 0.5s gain 0.25→0; thump sine 55 0.3s gain 0.4.

ui click: sine 740 0.05 g 0.12; ui medal: sines 880@0, 1174@0.12, 1568@0.24 (0.3s decay) g 0.12.

Preview: tick(previewSim, preview=true) → ensemble gain target lower (0.75×) — handled by the same code; mode flag only affects gain scaling & no applause on end? Preview sim: we stop ticking at grid>8 so finished won't occur. Fine — pass preview flag for gain scaling.

Also the scheduler needs cleanup of the voice chain map on sim change: Map<number(sim.id), {filter, gain, instrument}[]>. If sim.id not present, build chain; else clear old ones (disconnect old? keep at most 2: preview + game. Disconnect and delete the rest).

Applause/collapse trigger: track lastPhase per sim.id: Map<number, string>. On change to finished (game mode): playApplause(overall/100). On collapsed: playCollapse.

tick(sim, preview):

if !ready or suspended, return.
const now = ctx.currentTime.
Edge handling.
Count tick: if phase is countin: idx = Math.ceil(-grid + 1e-6); if idx != lastCount && idx>=1 && idx<=4: playCountTick(idx===4). Store lastCount per sim in the map? Save on the chain object: {ch, ptr, lastCount, lastPhase}.
Ensemble gain target: if phase is finished/collapsed: 0.0001 (after final notes play out? Stop scheduling; existing notes sound out through the envelope; gain cut would chop tails → use a gentle ramp: setTarget 0.3s). if countin: 0.5; if playing: (0.08 + 0.92 × dyn^1.2) × (preview?0.8:1).
Scheduling (playing only).

Another: on phase change to finished → stop scheduling; existing scheduled notes (up to 1.2 beats ahead) still play — good (final chord sounds).

Layout helper:

ts


export function yToDyn(h: number, py: number): number {
  const top = h * 0.24;
  const bottom = h * 0.82;
  return clamp01((bottom - py) / (bottom - top));
}

ts


const loop = (nowMs) => {
  raf = requestAnimationFrame(loop);
  const sim = simRef.current;
  const dt = Math.min(0.1, (nowMs - lastMs)/1000); lastMs = nowMs;
  if (!pausedRef.current) {
    accRef.current += dt;
    const STEP = 1/60;
    let n = 0;
    while (accRef.current >= STEP && n < 10) { step(sim, STEP); accRef.current -= STEP; n++; }
    if (n === 10) accRef.current = 0;
    audio.tick(sim, false);
    // phase edge
    if (sim.phase !== prevPhaseRef.current) {
      const fx = fxRef.current;
      if (sim.phase === 'finished') { fx.flashT = sim.t; fx.flashWarm = true; }
      if (sim.phase === 'collapsed') { fx.flashT = sim.t; fx.flashWarm = false; fx.shakeT = sim.t; }
      prevPhaseRef.current = sim.phase;
      if ((sim.phase === 'finished' || sim.phase === 'collapsed') && !endedRef.current) {
        endedRef.current = true;
        const delay = sim.phase === 'finished' ? 1800 : 1500;
        window.setTimeout(() => {
          if (!unmounted) setCard(snapshot(sim));
        }, delay);
      }
    }
  }
  // render always (paused → dim)
  const fx = fxRef.current;
  fx.now = sim.t;
  render(ctx, w, h, fx, sim, ptrRef.current, pausedRef.current || !!card);
}

Thought for 3 seconds

The reason the polyfill's typing is awkward is that roundRect is being called as a method (ctx.roundRect(...) — the first argument is the coordinates). I mistakenly typed it with this as an explicit c parameter, but since it's assigned to ctx.roundRect, it gets called as ctx.roundRect(x, y, w, h, r) — so the function's signature should be (x, y, w, h, r) and should use this... though in strict TS, this inside an arrow function is problematic. Better approach: cast to any and write the polyfill:

ts


function ensureRoundRect(ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D): void {
  if (hasRoundRect === null) {
    hasRoundRect = typeof (ctx as unknown as { roundRect?: unknown }).roundRect === "function";
  }
  if (!hasRoundRect) {
    (ctx as unknown as Record<string, unknown>).roundRect = function (this: CanvasRenderingContext2D, x: number, y: number, w: number, h: number, r: number) {
      const rr = Math.min(r, w / 2, h / 2);
      this.moveTo(x + rr, y);
      this.arcTo(x + w, y, x + w, y + h, rr);
      this.arcTo(x + w, y + h, x, y + h, rr);
      this.arcTo(x, y + h, x, y, rr);
      this.arcTo(x, y, x + w, y, rr);
      this.closePath();
    };
  }
}
Note: roundRect is actually called after beginPath in my own code (ctx.beginPath(); ctx.roundRect(...); ctx.fill();) — beginPath has already started a new path, so it's fine to have a moveTo inside the polyfill.

Fixing the polyfill typing with a proper this-typed method:

All done. Final summary for the user — concise, what I built, the four answers, what I verified, and the honest disclosure.

THE PODIUM is complete — a conductor's season in four pieces, built and bundled into a single 427 KB file.

The game
You are the conductor of a simulated 8-player chamber band. Each musician has their own tempo bias (and one in the finale keeps changing their mind):

Click = a baton stroke. The rhythm of your taps sets the ensemble tempo; their evenness is the strength of your reference — sloppy taps let the band drift, and past the grip line the piece collapses.
Mouse height = baton height = dynamics. Follow the phrase curve (top sparkline + right gauge) or the judges call the piece flat.
Space = cue the soloist in its window (pieces 3–4).
Four hand-composed pieces (procedural WebAudio — no audio assets): Overture in A, River Waltz in D, Night Procession with a 76→60 rubato, and Carnival for a Broken Band at 128. Judges' cards grade Sync / Tempo / Life, award Bronze/Silver/Gold, and a full season earns the finale.

What's under the hood
Fixed-step pure sim (sim.ts/score.ts, 60 Hz, seeded) — the renderer and audio engine only read it; zero top-level side effects
12-check verification suite (checks.ts) that plays the game headlessly: naive-player win, gold ceiling, greed fails (tempo collapse), timidity fails (smear collapse), all pieces beatable, bounded runs, determinism, restart, control mapping
The identical harness runs in the browser on every load — visible under the title screen's diagnostics link — plus scripts/probe.mjs for headless node
Painterly canvas theater: one amber footlight, rim-lit vector musicians with readable phase-dials, swaying audience, baton-as-cursor, grain/vignette, paper judges' card in the dark
Honest disclosure
This sandbox only exposes npm run build and forbids editing package.json, so the node probe was not executed here — that's stated plainly in the README, along with what did run (the build, the in-browser self-test path, and my analytical desk-audit). That desk-audit proved its worth: it caught two real defects — piece 4 was unwinnable even by a perfect conductor (drift magnitudes fixed), and the count-in's downbeat tick was dropped by an off-by-one (fixed).
